item.title: Data Security Startup Matters.AI Nets ₹115 Cr From Tanglin Venture Partners, Others
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: AI-native data security platform Matters.AI (formerly OptiQ.AI) has raised ₹115 Cr ($12.0 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led…
item.content:encoded:
AI-native data security platform Matters.AI (formerly OptiQ.AI) has raised ₹115 Cr ($12.0 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Tanglin Venture Partners. 

IIFL Fintech Fund, Piper Serica’s Bharat Tech Fund, Foster Ventures, and Tetration Ventures also joined the startup’s cap table, while existing investors Kalaari Capital and Endiya Partners doubled down on their earlier bet on the Bengaluru-based AI startup. 

The startup will utilise the capital to accelerate R&D in data lineage, autonomous investigation, endpoint and browser intelligence, and prevention of sensitive data misuse by AI agents. It is also expanding its North American sales operations and leadership. 

“Enterprise data security is at an inflection point. As AI agents increasingly operate alongside humans, the challenge is no longer just knowing where sensitive data resides, but understanding how it’s being used and acting before it becomes a risk,” said Tanglin’s managing partner Sankalp Gupta. 

Founded in 2023 by Keshava Murthy and Harsh Sahu, Matters.AI builds an autonomous “AI Security Engineer for Data” powered by its Data Detection and Response (DDR) platform. 

Matters.AI operates teams across Bengaluru and the San Francisco Bay Area. The startup claims to serve over 50 clients including major financial institutions, stockbroking firms, asset managers, retailers, and digital media platforms. It has raised around ₹175 Cr till date, including the latest round. 

As enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents, Matters’ platform helps identify sensitive data and trace how agents are moving it around by consolidating four typically fragmented enterprise functions – data security posture management, insider risk, activity monitoring, and data loss prevention – into a single platform. 

The platform discovers sensitive information across cloud, on-premises systems, SaaS applications, endpoints, and browsers. It tracks how the data moves using LLM-based fingerprinting, identifies risk signals and correlates them, and autonomously investigates and remediates policy violations.

With the latest advances in generative AI, frontier models are now increasingly being used to find vulnerabilities and exploits in software within a fraction of the time it once took. The integration of AI into these systems, if not implemented with careful data governance and visibility, can create even more entry points for attackers. 

Concerns around cybersecurity have only become more prominent in recent weeks with disruptions to the tech infrastructure used by Microsoft, Apple, JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Earlier this week, SaaS startup MoEngage, too, saw its cloud infrastructure breached via a compromised third-party vendor account.

item.title: Zavya Nets ₹22.6 Cr To Scale Everyday Silver Jewellery Biz
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Budget jewellery startup Zavya has raised ₹22.6 Cr ($2.4 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Daksham Growth…
item.content:encoded:
Budget jewellery startup Zavya has raised ₹22.6 Cr ($2.4 Mn) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Daksham Growth Ventures (DGV), the growth investment arm of Daksham Capital, with participation from existing investor Orios Venture Partners.

The investment values the silver jewellery brand at approximately ₹191.5 Cr on a post-money basis.

“With DGV joining us and Orios continuing to back us, we are excited to strengthen our presence across D2C and quick commerce, invest in long-term brand building and take our first steps into physical retail,” Zavya cofounder and CEO Poem Kabra said.

Founded in  2021 by Kabra and Ravi Malani, Zavya offers silver jewellery targeted for 22-35 year old women. Its everyday 925 sterling silver jewelry, including products like individual rings, pendants, earrings, and anklets, are priced between ₹699-2,299. The startup claims to come up with over 50 new styles every month. 

Zavya operates through its own website and mobile application, alongside quick commerce platforms such as Blinkit and Zepto. It also sells through online marketplaces including Amazon, Myntra and Nykaa.

For the fiscal year FY25, Zavya reported a net profit of ₹54.7 Lakh on a revenue of ₹6 Cr (up 38% YoY). While numbers for further periods are yet to be determined, the brand claims to have maintained EBITDA profitability while scaling. 

The five-year old brand sees a robust opportunity in scaling in the world’s largest silver jewellery market by fabrication volume. 

A report by Credence Research estimates India’s 925 sterling silver jewellery D2C market at $614 Mn in 2025 and projects it to reach $2.28 Bn by 2035, growing at a CAGR of 14%. The report identifies online channels as the largest distribution segment, accounting for 60% of market value in 2025, while quick commerce is expected to be among the faster-growing channels.

In this market, Zavya competes with legacy Beliram Legacy, TrueSilver, and Silver Emporium. Meanwhile, it is one of the up and coming new-age jewellery brands that bid to capitalise on the growing market opportunity and challenge the incumbents. Backed by strong venture capital backing, brands like Giva and Palmonas are also bidding to take on legacy giants with their select, premium-feel offerings at more affordable price ranges.

item.title: Sarvam AI Defends Token Factory, Says Homegrown Models Remain Core Focus
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than…
item.content:encoded:
AI unicorn Sarvam AI has defended its Token Factory business, saying the platform runs on privately procured GPUs rather than government-subsidised computing capacity, while reiterating that developing homegrown AI models remains its core focus.

In a post on X, cofounder Pratyush Kumar addressed questions about the startup’s government support, its decision to host global open-weight models, and whether its expansion into inference infrastructure signals a shift away from building indigenous models.

Notably, Token Factory’s launch had sparked online debates about Sarvam’s use of government subsidised compute capacity and its ability to anchor India’s indigenous AI ambitions. 

Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission gave around 20 startups access to GPUs at a 40% discount. Sarvam used this computing capacity to train its 105-billion-parameter foundation model from scratch, completing and releasing it in February 2026, he said.

He added that the government did not make direct payments to Sarvam. Instead, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, which supplied discounted computing resources to participating startups.

Sarvam’s access to the government-supported GPU allocation ended in March this year. The startup said Token Factory operates on GPUs it procured privately.

Under the IndiaAI Mission, Sarvam received access to 4,096 Nvidia H100 GPUs to develop indigenous foundation models. The six-month computing allocation was valued at around ₹247 Cr, including a government subsidy of ₹98.68 Cr.

The Inference Business Case

The clarification follows the launch of Token Factory, which hosts Sarvam’s own models alongside global open-weight models, including Google’s Gemma and China’s DeepSeek and Kimi, on GPU infrastructure in India.

The platform lets developers and enterprises access multiple models through a single API, without procuring GPUs or managing model deployment themselves. It charges customers for the tokens they use.

Kumar said open-weight models offer enterprises cost advantages and greater control over their AI systems. However, Indian businesses requiring data to remain within the country and fast responses for interactive applications need access to locally hosted models, he argued.

He claimed Sarvam has optimised its data centre-scale inference infrastructure to offer token prices comparable to or lower than global providers such as Fireworks AI, Baseten, and Together AI.

Kumar said India consumes a few trillion tokens daily, with most of this demand served from overseas. Building domestic inference capacity could reduce that dependence while creating a commercial opportunity, he argued.

He added that Sarvam would continue reducing costs and widening access to inference services in India.

Sarvam Reiterates Focus On Homegrown Models

Kumar said building inference infrastructure does not conflict with Sarvam’s core mission of training its own models.

Over the past few months, the startup has optimised its training systems for NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs alongside building Token Factory and expanding its enterprise offerings, he said.

Using this infrastructure, Sarvam trained Sarvam-105B-1711, an upgraded version of its 105-billion-parameter model, which it released yesterday.

The company claimed improvements in reasoning, tool use, Indian languages, and work tasks involving multiple steps. Kumar described it as one of the strongest models in the Flash-Lite category, which targets high-volume applications such as customer support and voice agents.

Kumar said the model can power its agentic AI product Indus. Alongside the model weights, Sarvam is releasing training and inference recipes to help developers build on the technology.

The startup plans to release more models across vision, speech, and edge AI over the next two weeks. It is also working with partners to bring the latest training-grade computing infrastructure to India for its next generation of larger models.

Kumar said Sarvam aims to pursue larger models while building a sustainable commercial business serving enterprises and population-scale applications.

item.title: Congress Protests Against Meta’s Content Moderation Practices, Political Bias
item.dc:creator: Md Zakariya Khan
item.description: The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have once again raised questions over social media giant…
item.content:encoded:
The ongoing protests by members of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) have once again raised questions over social media giant Meta’s content moderation policies. 

The demonstrations by  IYC workers in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram come amid an allegedly sharp increase in the volume of content restricted by Meta in India under local laws. The company restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items on Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, as per Meta’s latest transparency disclosures.

The surge represents a roughly 131-fold increase over the preceding six-month period, placing India among Meta’s largest markets for government-mandated content restrictions. 

The restrictions covered several categories, including content relating to online gaming, synthetically generated material depicting prominent figures, threats to India’s sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups.

The data has put the spotlight on India’s evolving regulatory framework for social media platforms, particularly the tightening of timelines for content removal and the growing use of automated systems to enforce government directions.

The Controversy

Protesters have alleged that Meta is selectively enforcing its content moderation policies and removing posts and accounts critical of the central government. The primary accusation against the US-based company is its bias towards Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Case in point was the removal or restriction of Instagram accounts linked to opposition figures. Congress has demanded an explanation for these actions as well as restoration of  affected accounts.

The opposition has also questioned the role of Meta’s recommendation and moderation algorithms and sought clarity on identification and flagging of said political content.

As per Meta, its content moderation framework combines automated detection systems, human review and enforcement of local legal requirements. However, when restrictions are imposed following government requests, users may not always have sufficient information about the authority behind a takedown or the specific legal provision invoked.

This creates a transparency challenge.

Meta has declined to comment on the protests and Congress’ allegations of politically motivated restrictions. The company has maintained that it restricts content in India to comply with applicable local laws.

Nevertheless, the scale of restrictions has intensified concerns about the potential for overblocking, where legitimate content could also become inaccessible because of automated enforcement.

India’s Laws Governing Social Media Takedowns

India’s social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, intermediaries are required to remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer.

The provisions cover content that threatens India’s sovereignty and integrity, national security, public order, friendly relations with foreign countries, or relates to defamation, contempt of court, decency and morality, among other grounds.

The framework allows the government to direct platforms to restrict specific posts, URLs or other online content. Platforms are required to comply with these directions to retain the legal protections available to intermediaries under Section 79 of the IT Act.

However, the government has also introduced additional safeguards and compliance obligations over the past year.

In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments to Rule 3(1)(d), which came into effect on November 15, 2025.

The amendments mandated that government takedown notices be issued by senior authorised officials and clearly specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content to be restricted.

They also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials to assess whether the restrictions remain necessary and proportionate.

In February 2026, the government tightened the compliance timeline further. An amendment effective February 20 reduced the deadline for intermediaries to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to just three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation.

The shorter deadline has increased the pressure on platforms to maintain automated content detection and enforcement systems capable of responding to government directions within a narrow window.

item.title: Bengaluru Green SM Protests: Police Book Protesters For Vandalism
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among…
item.content:encoded:
Police authorities in Bengaluru’s Electronic City have reportedly registered an FIR against Karnataka Chalakara Okkuta’s president G Narayana Swamy, among others, for destroying recruitment posters of Green SM.

Swamy and his group of unidentified cab drivers allegedly barged into a private hotel in Hosa Road and vandalised the property by tearing up banners, abusing company representatives, in a bid to impede the Vietnamese ride-hailing firm’s recruitment drive.

As per a report by the Deccan Herald, the FIR was registered suo motu under five sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) relating to property damage, unlawful assembly, intentional insult, breach of peace and criminal intimidation.

Inc42 has not been able to source the FIR so far. We have reached out to Green SM for comments on this development. The story will be updated based on their response.

This comes about a week after the state government directed transport department officials to stop registering new Green SM taxis until further orders, even as around 100 vehicles operated by the company have already been registered to ply on Karnataka roads. 

The e-taxi operator, part of Vietnam’s Vingroup, which also operates electric car OEM Vinfast, received an aggregator licence from the Karnataka Transport Department earlier this month.

The issuance of the same triggered protests across the state. Bengaluru-based private transport associations such as Karnataka Rajya Chalakara Parishath and Peace Auto Union demand protection citing interests of local taxi owners and drivers.

Yet, the state government is yet to take a final call on whether Green SM will be allowed to continue its operations in Karnataka.

However, the transport department is said to be planning to make fare meters compulsory for all cabs, including those operating through ride-hailing platforms such as Uber and Rapido.

Green SM started India operations in June this year. It is already operational in Delhi NCR and Hyderabad and touched the 15 Lakh rides milestone earlier this month. 

The issues in Karnataka come at a time when it is preparing to expand across six new geographies. The firm has also secured aggregator licences in Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh.
